title: Caching Strategies & Layers
summary: Caching trades freshness for speed at every layer of the stack — browser, CDN, reverse proxy, application, and database. The right strategy depends on read/write ratios, consistency tolerance, and failure modes. Poor cache design causes stale data bugs, thundering herds, and memory exhaustion.

sections.title: Why and Where to Cache
paragraphs: Caching stores copies of expensive-to-compute or expensive-to-fetch data closer to the consumer. A database query taking 50 ms might be served from Redis in 1 ms or from a browser cache in 0 ms. At scale, caching is not optional — it is how systems survive.

Caches exist at multiple layers. Browser caches use HTTP headers (Cache-Control, ETag). CDNs cache static assets and cacheable API responses at edge PoPs globally. Reverse proxies (Nginx, Varnish) cache upstream responses. Application caches (Redis, Memcached) hold hot keys in memory. Database buffer pools cache pages internally.

Each layer has different TTL semantics, invalidation mechanisms, and consistency guarantees. A coherent caching strategy defines what is cached where, how long it lives, and how it is invalidated when source data changes.

sections.title: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back
paragraphs: Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application checks the cache first. On miss, it loads from the database, populates the cache, and returns. On write, the application updates the database and deletes or updates the cache entry. This is the most common pattern — simple and flexible.

Write-through: every write goes to cache and database synchronously. Reads always hit warm cache. Consistency is strong between cache and DB, but writes are slower. Used when read-heavy workloads demand guaranteed cache freshness.

Write-back (write-behind): writes go to cache first; cache asynchronously flushes to the database. Maximizes write throughput but risks data loss if the cache fails before flush. Suitable for write-heavy, eventually-durable workloads like buffering analytics events.
bullets: Cache-aside: app manages cache; best general-purpose pattern
Write-through: synchronous DB + cache write; strong consistency
Write-back: async flush; high write throughput, durability risk

sections.title: Invalidation and the Thundering Herd
paragraphs: Cache invalidation is notoriously difficult. Time-based expiry (TTL) is simple but serves stale data until expiry. Event-driven invalidation (pub/sub, message queues) is precise but requires wiring every write path to emit invalidation events.

The thundering herd (cache stampede) occurs when a popular key expires and thousands of concurrent requests miss the cache simultaneously, each hitting the database. Mitigations include probabilistic early expiration, request coalescing (single-flight pattern), and mutex locks per key.

Versioned cache keys (e.g., product:123:v5) allow atomic invalidation by bumping a version counter instead of deleting keys. Negative caching stores 'not found' results to protect against repeated lookups for missing entities.

sections.title: Distributed Caching with Redis
paragraphs: Redis and Memcached provide shared, in-memory caches accessible to all application instances. Redis adds persistence options, rich data structures, pub/sub, and Lua scripting for atomic operations.

Size caches appropriately: too small causes constant eviction and low hit rates; too large wastes memory and money. Monitor hit rate, eviction rate, memory usage, and latency p99. Target 90%+ hit rates for well-chosen keys.

Redis Cluster and client-side consistent hashing distribute keys across shards. Hot keys — a single key receiving disproportionate traffic — require replication, local caching, or key splitting strategies.

deepDive.title: Caching Strategies & Layers — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating Caching Strategies & Layers well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey

deepDive.title: Caching Strategies & Layers — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around Caching Strategies & Layers often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: Caching Strategies & Layers — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, Caching Strategies & Layers interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

concepts: Cache hit vs miss and hit rate as primary metric
CDN edge caching and Cache-Control headers
ETag and conditional requests for bandwidth savings
Redis data structures: strings, hashes, sorted sets
Hot key problem in distributed caches
Cache penetration, breakdown, and avalanche scenarios
practices: Set TTLs on every cache entry — unbounded caches grow until they crash
Use single-flight or locking to prevent thundering herds on hot keys
Cache at the highest layer possible (CDN before Redis before DB)
Monitor hit rate, eviction rate, and memory; alert on sudden drops
Invalidate or version keys on write — do not rely on TTL alone for critical data
Size Redis with headroom for peak traffic and avoid maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru without understanding evictions
Test cache failure modes: what happens when Redis is entirely unavailable?
pitfalls: Caching without TTL and running out of memory
Invalidating cache after DB write fails — serving stale data indefinitely
Caching large objects that evict the entire working set
Ignoring cache consistency during database failover
Using the same TTL for rapidly changing and static data
Caching personalized data at CDN layer without Vary headers

examples.title: Product catalog with CDN + Redis
examples.description: Product images and static JSON are CDN-cached with 24-hour TTL. Product details are cache-aside in Redis with 5-minute TTL and event invalidation on price updates. Search results are not cached — they change too frequently and are user-specific.

examples.title: Leaderboard with write-back
examples.description: Game scores write to Redis sorted sets immediately for real-time leaderboard display. A background job flushes aggregated scores to PostgreSQL every 30 seconds. Acceptable data loss window: 30 seconds of scores if Redis fails — mitigated by Redis persistence (AOF).

examples.title: Preventing thundering herd on flash sale
examples.description: A popular product key uses single-flight: on cache miss, one request fetches from DB while others wait on the same promise. Combined with probabilistic early refresh (refresh at 90% of TTL), the DB never sees a spike of 10,000 concurrent queries.

keyTakeaways: Cache at every layer — browser, CDN, app, database buffer pool
Cache-aside is the default; write-through when read consistency is critical
Invalidation is harder than population — design it with every write path
Guard against thundering herds with single-flight and early expiration
Monitor hit rates and plan for cache cluster failures
Not everything should be cached — skip highly volatile or personalized data
whyItMatters: A well-designed cache reduces database load by 10–100× and cuts user-facing latency dramatically. A poorly designed cache causes subtle stale-data bugs that are hard to reproduce and catastrophic overload events when caches fail open. Caching appears in virtually every system design interview and every production performance investigation.
reflectionQuestions: What happens during a cache stampede when a popular key expires?
When is write-through preferable to cache-aside?
How would you cache user-specific data without serving one user's data to another?
What is your fallback when the entire Redis cluster is down?
